name: Poland
subtitle: Pilot country for the EU membership-impact project. Annual view from 1996 (two years before accession negotiations opened) through negotiations (1998–2002), entry (1 May 2004) and today. Five lenses: legal, financial, commercial, political, social.

legal.title: Adopting the acquis (1994–2004)
paras: Membership required Poland to absorb the entire body of EU law — the acquis communautaire, negotiated across ~30 chapters between 1998 and 2002. This drove a wholesale harmonisation of Polish legislation before entry: competition and state-aid rules, environmental standards, food safety, public procurement, consumer protection, border and customs law. Pre-accession restructuring of coal and steel had to conform to EU state-aid discipline before day one.

The 1997 Constitution was written with membership in view: Articles 90–91 permit the transfer of competences to an international organisation and give ratified treaties precedence over national statutes — the domestic legal basis for EU law's direct effect in Poland.

legal.title: Inside the Union: supremacy and its limits (2004–2015)
paras: From 1 May 2004 EU regulations applied directly and Polish courts began referring questions to the Court of Justice of the EU. Poland's Constitutional Tribunal accepted membership but — like Germany's — reserved the Constitution's position as supreme domestic law, a tension that stayed theoretical for a decade.

legal.title: The rule-of-law conflict (2015–2023)
paras: Judicial overhauls from late 2015 (Constitutional Tribunal appointments, court restructuring, a Disciplinary Chamber for judges) triggered the Commission's rule-of-law framework in January 2016 and, on 20 December 2017, the first-ever activation of Article 7(1) TEU against a member state. The CJEU ruled repeatedly against the disciplinary regime; in October 2021 Poland's Constitutional Tribunal ruled parts of the EU treaties unconstitutional — a direct challenge to the primacy of EU law — and the CJEU imposed a €1m-per-day penalty (later halved) for keeping the Disciplinary Chamber running. Recovery-fund and cohesion money was withheld.

legal.title: Resolution (2022–2024)
paras: A June 2022 law abolished the Disciplinary Chamber; after the 2023 change of government, Poland met the Commission's "super milestones" on judicial independence. On 29 February 2024 the Commission unblocked up to €137bn (€59.8bn recovery funds + €76.5bn cohesion), and on 29 May 2024 the Article 7 procedure was closed.
legal.note: Net effect over the window: Polish law was first massively harmonised toward EU norms (1994–2004), then became the EU's main testing ground for what happens when a member state contests EU law's primacy — ending with EU financial leverage proving decisive.

financial.title: The headline
paras: Poland went from 45% of average EU income in 1996 to ~83% in 2025 (PPP), was the only EU economy to avoid recession in 2009, and received net EU transfers averaging roughly 2–3.5% of GDP per year after entry (€161.8bn net, 2004–2023). Unemployment peaked at 20.2% in 2002 just before entry and sits near 3% today — among the EU's lowest.

charts.title: Long-term government bond yield, %
charts.sub: Eurostat EMU convergence-criterion series: yield on ten-year government bonds. Poland's fell from 10.68% in 2001 to a low of 1.50% in 2020, then rose to 5.52% by 2025.

charts.title: Net annual earnings, €
charts.sub: Single person, no children, on 100% of the average wage. Eurostat flags 2024 as a break in series, so 2000–2023 and 2024–2025 are two segments rather than one line.

commercial.title: Single-market integration
paras: Trade openness transformed: exports rose from 22% of GDP (1996) to a peak of 62% (2022). The large majority of Poland's goods exports go to other EU states, with Germany by far the largest single partner (≈ share varies by year — see method note). Inside the single market Poland became one of Europe's leading production bases for automotive components, home appliances and furniture, and after 2004 a major nearshoring destination for services.

EU competition and state-aid rules have applied in full since 2004, ending the discretionary industrial subsidies of the transition era; accession itself was conditional on restructuring coal and steel under state-aid discipline.

commercial.title: Trade in goods & services, % of GDP
commercial.sub: Exports and imports of goods and services. Poland ran persistent deficits before accession; exports overtook imports for most years after 2013.

charts.title: FDI net inflows, % of GDP
charts.sub: Foreign direct investment. Pre-accession privatisation wave (1998–2000), then post-entry surges 2004–07 and 2021–22.

charts.title: International arrivals, millions
charts.sub: World Bank / UNWTO border arrivals incl. same-day visitors. Counting methodology changed around 2000–01; series ends 2019.

political.title: How membership reshaped the political landscape
paras: 1991–2004: EU entry was the consensus goal of every government, left and right — the SLD-PSL and AWS-UW governments negotiated and closed the deal; the referendum passed 3-to-1.

2004–2015: Politics reorganised around the pace and terms of integration rather than membership itself. Civic Platform (PO) under Donald Tusk (PM 2007–2014) positioned Poland as a core EU player; Tusk became President of the European Council (2014–2019). Law and Justice (PiS) built a sovereigntist counter-pole while never advocating exit.

2015–2023: The PiS governments' judicial overhaul turned relations with Brussels into the central axis of Polish politics — Article 7, CJEU fines and frozen funds became domestic campaign issues. Membership support stayed high throughout; the dispute was about EU authority, not EU membership.

2023–today: The October 2023 election returned a pro-EU coalition under Tusk; funds were unblocked within months and Poland held the Council presidency in the first half of 2025. The presidency remains a counterweight: Karol Nawrocki, backed by PiS, won the June 2025 presidential election.
political.note: Structural change: EU accession created a durable pro-integration vs sovereigntist cleavage that has organised Polish party competition since 2004 — while support for membership itself has never been seriously contested.

social.title: Migration: out, then in
paras: The post-2004 exodus: free movement opened the UK, Irish and Swedish labour markets on day one. GUS estimates put Poles living temporarily abroad at over 2 million at the peak — one of the largest intra-EU migrations ever — easing unemployment at home and generating substantial remittances.

The reversal: from the mid-2010s Poland itself became a major immigration destination, first for Ukrainian workers, then — after Russia's February 2022 invasion — as the EU's principal first-arrival refugee host, with around 1 million Ukrainians under temporary protection. The 2022 spike dominates the chart below.

social.title: Net migration, thousands of people
social.sub: UN World Population Prospects estimates via World Bank. Blue = net inflow, red = net outflow. Post-2022 values are heavily model-revised (refugee movements and returns) — treat recent years as indicative.

charts.title: Income inequality (Gini index)
charts.sub: World Bank estimate (0 = perfect equality). Inequality rose through transition, peaked around accession, then fell to below the EU norm.

charts.title: Net migration per 1,000 residents
charts.sub: The same flow scaled by population, which is the comparable form — the chart above is a headcount and so partly tracks country size.

prose.title: Welfare & living standards
paras: The Gini decline from ~38 (2004) to ~28.5 (2023) reflects tight labour markets, EU-supported rural incomes (CAP direct payments), minimum-wage growth and the "500+" child benefit (2016; raised to 800 PLN in 2024), which sharply cut child poverty.

EU cohesion money — €161bn of the €245.5bn received through 2023 — rebuilt infrastructure: the motorway/expressway network expanded several-fold after 2004, and EU co-financing touched rail, water, broadband and universities in every region.

method.title: Window
method.text: Negotiations opened 31 March 1998, so the observation window starts in 1996 (−2 years per project rule) and runs to the latest available year (2025 for most series).

method.title: Data pipeline
method.text: This page is generated by build_dashboard.py from data/indicators.csv (tidy long format: iso3, indicator, year, value, source, retrieved), data/milestones.csv and data/narrative/<ISO3>.json. Nothing is hard-coded in the HTML — adding a country means appending rows and one narrative file.

method.title: Confidence rule
method.text: Per project instructions everything shown is held at ≥95% confidence and traceable to the sources above. Items marked (≈) are range or order-of-magnitude statements (EU share of exports, polling ranges) that are well documented directionally but vary by year and survey — verify before quoting precisely.

method.title: Known data caveats
method.text: Tourism arrivals: counting methodology changed around 2000–01 (same-day border traffic) and the series is discontinued after 2019 — levels are not comparable across the break. Net migration: UN model estimates with major post-2022 revisions. Gini: World Bank income-survey estimate; Eurostat's EU-SILC Gini differs slightly in level. 2025 values are the World Bank's current published figures and may be revised.

method.title: Attribution caution
method.text: Charts show what happened around membership, not what membership alone caused. Poland's trajectory mixes EU effects with transition reforms begun in 1990, global cycles and domestic policy. Where causal claims are established in the literature (cohesion funding scale, trade integration, post-2004 emigration), the text says so; otherwise read the series as context.
